archetype.name: Retooling (special-teams dependent)
archetype.definition: A club that was a top-five team on the site a few seasons ago and has now sunk to the bottom tier for a second straight year, held up by an excellent power play and penalty kill but without the 5-on-5 play or finishing to climb back.

report.headline: Elite special teams can't hide a losing 5-on-5 team that can't finish
report.take:
Calgary is 9-11-1 and 26th of 32 on the site, and the record flatters it. The Flames have scored 51 and allowed 74, a -23 differential that ranks 30th per game. They sit 29th in goals for and 27th in goals against, so there is no strong half to build on. The pace is 74 standings points, a near-repeat of last season's 77, when the offense ranked dead last. The slide from 111 points in 2021-22 has not reversed.

The one thing working is special teams, and it works very well. The power play converts 27.1% (5th), against a league average of 22.2% and last year's 16.2%. The penalty kill holds at 82.8% (9th). Joel Farabee (9 PP points) and Matt Coronato (7) drive most of that. At 5-on-5 the picture flips. Calgary breaks even on shot attempts (CF % 50%, 12th) but gets only 46.4% of the expected goals (25th). It holds the puck and generates little that is dangerous. Mikael Backlund has 3 goals on 52 shots and Ryan Strome 3 on 44: a lot of volume, not much quality.

Two kinds of luck are pulling in opposite directions. The skaters are shooting 9.0% in all situations, 31st, against a league mark of 11.4%. The 5-on-5 PDO of 95.9 is badly depressed, so some goals should come back. Against that, Pts vs Goal Diff is +3.1, 2nd in the league: the Flames have banked points in one-goal and overtime games that their margins don't support. The likely result is a cleaner differential but not a better record.

The bigger structural change is in goal. Team GSAx was +16.7 and +14.2 the last two seasons, and goaltending was what kept those teams respectable. This year it is -4 (25th). The split is stark. Devin Cooley (.906, +1.5 GSAx) has been fine, while Dustin Wolf (.875, -5.7) has been one of the league's weaker starters over his 10 starts. With a D-graded blueline in front of them (Zayne Parekh -14, Simon Nemec -11, both with xGF % below 45-49%), Calgary cannot afford below-average goaltending. That is the difference between last year's mediocrity and this year's drift toward the lottery.

strengths.title: A top-five power play
strengths.body: Calgary converts 27.1% of its power plays, well above the league's 22.2% and a big jump from last season's 16.2%. Farabee and Coronato carry most of the production. Rates this far above the team's own history usually cool, so expect a good unit rather than an elite one over 61 more games.

strengths.title: Penalty kill is genuinely good
strengths.body: The PK sits 9th at 82.8%, ahead of the league's 77.4% and in line with the 80-83% range Calgary has posted most seasons. That history makes it the most bankable part of the team.

strengths.title: Possession is not the problem
strengths.body: A CF % of 50% (12th) and league-average shot volume mean the Flames are not getting caved in on attempts. That leaves a floor to build on if shot quality improves. Right now it mostly produces perimeter volume.

concerns.title: Losing the chance battle at 5-on-5
concerns.body: Calgary owns only 46.4% of the expected goals (25th), and last season was similar at 47%. This is a chronic problem, not a slump. Even a rebound in shooting luck won't fix a team that consistently generates worse chances than it allows.

concerns.title: Goaltending lost its edge
concerns.body: The goalies were the backbone of the past two seasons, at +16.7 and +14.2 GSAx. This year they are -4 (25th), and almost all of the damage is Wolf's (-5.7, .875 save %). Cooley's +1.5 suggests the drop is goalie-specific rather than the defense collapsing.

concerns.title: Record already ahead of margin
concerns.body: A +3.1 Pts vs Goal Diff, 2nd in the league, means close-game and overtime results have propped up the standings. The -23 differential points to an even worse team. That kind of luck rarely holds.

trend.note: October was 2.57 scored and 3.71 allowed a game; November has tightened defensively (3.14 allowed) but the scoring has dipped to 2.14. The last 10 (4-5-1, .450) are almost exactly the season's level, though the last five allowed 3.8 a game, capped by a 1-6 loss in Anaheim.

weekAhead.headline: Two winnable games bracket Minnesota and a trip to Ottawa
weekAhead.body:
The week splits cleanly. San Jose and Chicago are teams Calgary should compete with or beat. San Jose ranks 29th in xGF % and allows 30.5 shots a game, and Calgary already won there 2-1. Chicago sits last in Goal Diff / GP at -1.85, with an .873 save % and the league's second-most generous defense against forwards. Minnesota is the opposite case. The Wild are 15-3-4, 2nd on the site, first in goals against and first in GSAx, and they allow the fewest points to forwards in the league. That is a terrible matchup for a team shooting 9%.

The Sunday trip to Ottawa is a coin flip with a specific angle. The Senators out-chance teams (xGF % 53.1%, 7th) but have the league's worst power play at 11.5%. Calgary's penalty kill takes away Ottawa's weak spot, while its own power play faces a 76% PK. Two wins is the realistic target, and three would be a good week.

keyMatchups.title: Feasting on Chicago's leaky defense
keyMatchups.body: Chicago allows forwards 1.48 points a game above expectation, ranked 31st, and gives up the second-most points to defensemen relative to expectation. The Blackhawks' .873 save % is 28th. If Calgary's cold finishers are going to turn, this is the game.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's goaltending wall
keyMatchups.body: The Wild lead the league in GSAx (+15.9) and save % (.917) and hold forwards furthest under their averages of any team. Against a Calgary offense ranked 29th, a low-event, low-scoring loss is the base case.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams edge in Ottawa
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa's 11.5% power play is last in the league and runs into Calgary's 9th-ranked kill. The Senators' 76% PK ranks 19th. It is the one area where the Flames clearly outclass a better team.

weekAhead.watch: Who gets the starts: Cooley's +1.5 GSAx against Wolf's -5.7 is the clearest lever Calgary has to steal games this week.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect slightly more goals and roughly the same standings fate. A 9.0% shooting rate is about as bad as it gets and should drift up, so 2.43 goals a game can climb. But an xGF % that has sat in the 46-47% range for two years caps the upside. Working the other way, the power play is running far above Calgary's history and the close-game luck (+3.1 points over the differential) should fade, which offsets much of the finishing gain. A finish of roughly 70-79 points is my projection, close to the current 74-point pace, with the differential improving from its current rate but staying clearly negative.

The swing piece is goaltending. If the crease returns to the level of the last two seasons, Calgary is a mid-70s-to-80-point team. If Wolf's numbers hold and he keeps splitting starts, the floor drops toward the low 70s. Nothing here suggests a playoff push in a Pacific Division led by Edmonton and Vegas.
swingFactors: Wolf's save % recovering toward Cooley's level
How far the power play cools

confidence.note: 21 games is a small sample, but the 5-on-5 weakness matches last season's profile.
